title: Gotchas and interview idioms cheat sheet
summary: A coding-round cheat sheet for TypeScript: the number, array, callback, string, date and JSON gotchas interviewers love, plus the short idioms that JavaScript forces on you — counting and grouping with `Map`, building grids safely, a pointer queue, a hand-rolled min-heap, multi-key comparators, `??=`, optional chaining and destructuring swaps.
prerequisiteNotes: ts-arrays-maps-sets: array methods, which ones mutate, `Map` versus objects and the default sort trap. This lesson assumes those and builds the interview toolkit on top; ts-equality-coercion covers `typeof`, `==` and floating point in depth.
objectives: Predict the classic JavaScript traps on sight: `0.1 + 0.2`, unsafe integers, `typeof null`, `map(parseInt)`, `for...in` on arrays, holes, shared `fill` rows, `JSON.stringify` drops, 0-based months, UTF-16 length, negative `%` and `return` on its own line.
Write the counting, grouping, grid, queue and swap idioms from memory without reaching for missing built-ins.
Implement a small generic binary min-heap and use it for top-k in O(n log k).
Compose a stable multi-key comparator with explicit tie-breaks and no `NaN` or truthiness traps.
Say which newer built-ins exist in the target (ES2023: `toSorted`, `at`, `findLast`) and which do not (`Map.groupBy`, `Object.groupBy` are ES2024).

concepts.title: Number gotchas: floats, safe integers, BigInt, % and truncation
concepts.body: Every `number` is a 64-bit float, so `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`; compare money in integer cents or with a tolerance. Integers are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1); products of two large ids or a factorial overflow silently, so use `bigint` (`10n`) and keep it away from `number` arithmetic (mixing throws). `%` is a **remainder** that takes the sign of the dividend: `-7 % 3` is `-1`, so circular indexes need `((i % n) + n) % n`. `Math.trunc` drops the fraction for any size; `x | 0` also truncates but first wraps to a signed 32-bit integer, so it breaks above 2^31. Use `Math.floor` for floor division of negatives (`Math.floor(-7 / 2)` is `-4`, `Math.trunc` gives `-3`). Numeric separators (`1_000_000`) are just readability. ts-equality-coercion covers `NaN` and `Number.isNaN` in depth.
concepts.code:
0.1 + 0.2;                        // 0.30000000000000004
Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON;  // true: compare with a tolerance

Number.isSafeInteger(Math.pow(2, 53));        // false
const big = 9_007_199_254_740_993n * 2n;       // exact bigint
// big + 1;                       // TypeError at runtime, compile error in TS

-7 % 3;                           // -1 (remainder keeps the dividend's sign)
const wrap = (i: number, n: number) => ((i % n) + n) % n;
wrap(-1, 5);                      // 4

Math.trunc(-7 / 2);               // -3
Math.floor(-7 / 2);               // -4
3_000_000_000 | 0;                // -1294967296: |0 wraps to int32
const mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1); // fine: indexes stay far below 2^31

concepts.title: Building arrays and grids: holes and shared rows
concepts.body: `new Array(3)` (or `Array(3)`) creates length 3 with **holes**, not `undefined` values: `map`, `forEach` and `filter` skip holes, so `Array(3).map((_, i) => i)` is still three holes. `Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => ...)` calls the mapper for every index and is the idiom for ranges and initialised arrays. The worse trap is `new Array(rows).fill(new Array(cols).fill(0))`: `fill` evaluates its argument **once** and stores the same row object in every slot, so writing `grid[0][0]` changes every row. Build grids with a factory per row: `Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(0))`; filling a row with a primitive is fine because primitives are copied. The same applies to `fill([])` for adjacency lists and `fill(new Set())` for buckets.

concepts.title: Callback and loop gotchas: map(parseInt), for...in, default sort
concepts.body: `map`, `filter` and `forEach` pass **three** arguments: value, index, array. Passing a function that has an optional second parameter changes its meaning: `['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)` calls `parseInt('2', 1)` with radix 1 and returns `[1, NaN, NaN]`. Wrap it (`s => parseInt(s, 10)`) or use `map(Number)`, which ignores extra arguments. `for...in` walks **enumerable string keys**, including inherited ones, so on an array it yields `'0'`, `'1'` as strings and `i + 1` concatenates; use `for...of` for values, `for (const [i, v] of arr.entries())` for both, and `Object.entries` for objects. And remember `sort()` with no comparator sorts as strings (`[10, 9, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 9]`) and mutates; ts-arrays-maps-sets covers it, here just always pass `(a, b) => a - b`.
concepts.code:
['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt);           // [1, NaN, NaN]
['1', '2', '3'].map(Number);             // [1, 2, 3]
['10', '7'].map(s => parseInt(s, 10));   // [10, 7]

const xs = [10, 20];
for (const i in xs) console.log(i + 1);   // '01', '11': keys are strings
for (const x of xs) console.log(x + 1);   // 11, 21
for (const [i, x] of xs.entries()) console.log(i, x);

[10, 9, 1].sort();                       // [1, 10, 9]
[10, 9, 1].toSorted((a, b) => a - b);    // [1, 9, 10], input untouched

concepts.title: Strings, dates, JSON and semicolons
concepts.body: `s.length` counts **UTF-16 code units**, so an emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane counts 2 and `s[i]` can return half of it; `[...s]` and `for...of` iterate code points (a skin-toned emoji is still two code points, and grapheme clusters need `Intl.Segmenter`). `typeof null` is `'object'`, so a null check must come first. In `Date`, months are **0-based** (`new Date(2024, 0, 31)` is 31 January) and setters roll over: setting month 1 on the 31st lands in March. `JSON.stringify` drops object properties whose value is `undefined`, a function or a symbol, writes them as `null` inside arrays, and turns `NaN` and `Infinity` into `null`; `Map` and `Set` become `{}`. Finally, automatic semicolon insertion ends a `return` at a line break, so `return` followed by the value on the next line returns `undefined`; keep the value or an opening bracket on the same line.

concepts.title: Idioms: count, group, default, swap
concepts.body: Count with a `Map`: `m.set(k, (m.get(k) ?? 0) + 1)`. A plain object works for string keys, but `'constructor'` and `'__proto__'` collide with `Object.prototype`, and numeric keys come back as strings and reordered. Group with get-or-create: `(groups.get(k) ?? groups.set(k, []).get(k)!).push(x)`, or on an object `(acc[k] ??= []).push(x)`. `Map.groupBy` and `Object.groupBy` are **ES2024** and not in an ES2023 target, so say that and write the four-line loop or `reduce`. `a ??= b` assigns only when `a` is `null` or `undefined` (unlike `||=`, it keeps `0` and `''`). Optional chaining short-circuits the whole chain: `node?.left?.val` is `undefined` if either link is missing, and `fn?.()` calls only if `fn` exists. Destructuring swaps without a temporary (`[a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]`), but a line that starts with `[` needs the previous statement to end in a semicolon.

concepts.title: Queues: a head pointer, not shift()
concepts.body: JavaScript has no deque. `push` is amortised O(1), but `shift()` removes index 0 and, per the spec, moves every remaining element down one, so a BFS that calls `shift()` per node is O(n²) in the worst case. Engines sometimes optimise small arrays, which is why it often looks fine in a demo and then times out. The interview idiom is a **head index**: push to the end, read `queue[head++]`, and loop while `head < queue.length`. Memory is not reclaimed until the array is dropped, which is fine for one BFS. For a long-lived queue, compact when `head` passes half the array, or use a ring buffer. For BFS levels, process `const size = queue.length - head` items per round. Use `pop()` freely: removing from the end is O(1), which is why an array is already a good stack.

concepts.title: A min-heap you can write in five minutes
concepts.body: There is no priority queue in the standard library, so top-k, Dijkstra, merging sorted streams and scheduling all need one. Store a complete binary tree in an array: the parent of `i` is `(i - 1) >> 1` and the children are `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`. `push` appends and **sifts up** while the new item beats its parent; `pop` saves the root, moves the last item to the root and **sifts down** to the better child. Both are O(log n), `peek` is O(1). Take a `less(a, b)` function instead of hard-coding numbers, so one class serves `[dist, node]` tuples, max-heaps (`(a, b) => a > b`) and tie-breaks. Sorting once is O(n log n) and fine when you need everything; the heap wins when you keep only k items or when items keep arriving.

walkthrough.title: Multi-key sorts: a comparator chain
walkthrough.body: When the order has several keys, write one small comparator per key and try them in turn: the first non-zero result decides. Keep each comparator honest: return a negative number, zero or a positive number, never a boolean (`a < b` coerces to 0 or 1 and gives a broken order). Avoid `a.time - b.time` when either side can be `null` or `Infinity`: `Infinity - Infinity` is `NaN`, which the sort treats as 0 and the order becomes arbitrary. Compare strings with `<` and `>` for code-unit order or with `localeCompare` for human order, and say which. `Array.prototype.sort` is **stable** since ES2019, so equal items keep their input order, but relying on that silently is a bug magnet; add the final tie-break explicitly.

walkthrough.title: Solve the core task: top-k words with a size-k heap
walkthrough.body: Say the plan in one breath: "count with a `Map`, keep a min-heap of the best k entries ordered by count then word, pop the weakest whenever the heap grows past k, then pop everything and reverse". The subtle part is the heap order: the root must be the entry you would throw away first, so for equal counts the **later** word is weaker. Counting is O(n); each of the u distinct words costs O(log k), so the total is O(n + u log k) time and O(u) space for the counts. Edge cases to name: `k = 0` returns `[]`, `k` larger than the number of distinct words returns all of them, and words such as `'constructor'` are safe because a `Map` has no prototype keys. If the interviewer says "just sort", that is O(u log u) and perfectly acceptable for small u; the heap is the answer to "what if the stream is huge and k is small?".

walkthrough.title: A 30-second gotcha sweep before you run
walkthrough.body: Read your code once for the traps in this lesson. Arrays: did any `fill` receive an object? Any `Array(n).map`? Loops: any `for...in` over an array? Callbacks: any `map(parseInt)` or comparator returning a boolean? Numbers: any `%` on a possibly negative index, `| 0` on a large value, or a product that can exceed 2^53? Truthiness: any `x || fallback` where `x` can legitimately be `0` or `''` (use `??`)? Strings: did you assume one character per code unit? Then trace one tiny input aloud. Interviewers notice the sweep as much as the fix.

task: Write `topKWords(words, k)`: return the `k` most frequent words, most frequent first, breaking ties by the word in ascending code-unit order (compare with `<`, so `'B'` comes before `'a'`). If there are fewer than `k` distinct words return them all; `k = 0` returns `[]`. JavaScript has no priority queue, so also write a generic class `MinHeap<T>` whose constructor takes `less(a, b): boolean` and which has `push(item)`, `pop(): T | undefined` and a `size` getter, and use it to keep **at most** `k` **entries** while you scan the counts, for O(n + u log k) time.
hints: The heap root should be the entry you would discard first: the lowest count, and for equal counts the word that sorts later. Push each `[word, count]` and pop whenever `size > k`.
When the scan ends the heap holds the k best entries, weakest on top. Pop them all into an array and reverse it to get best first.
checklist: Ties on count are broken by `<` on the word, so `'B'` precedes `'a'` and `'z'` precedes `'é'`.
The heap never holds more than k + 1 entries, and `k = 0` returns `[]`.
`MinHeap<T>` is generic with a `less` function, and `pop()` returns `undefined` when empty.
Counting uses a `Map`, so words like `'constructor'` are counted correctly.
pitfalls: Building a grid with `new Array(rows).fill(new Array(cols).fill(0))`, so every row is the same array.
Calling `arr.map(parseInt)`, which passes the index as the radix.
Using `for...in` on an array and doing arithmetic with string keys.
Using `queue.shift()` in BFS on large inputs; it is O(n) per call in the worst case.
Returning `a < b` from a comparator, or subtracting values that may be `null` or `Infinity`, which yields `NaN`.
Writing `x || fallback` when `0` or `''` is a valid value; use `??`.
Calling `Map.groupBy` or `Object.groupBy`, which are ES2024 and missing from an ES2023 runtime.
Treating `-1 % n` as a valid index, or using `| 0` on values beyond 2^31.

extraPractice.title: A grid builder that does not alias rows
extraPractice.prompt: Write a generic `makeGrid(rows, cols, init)` that returns a `T[][]` where cell `[r][c]` is `init(r, c)`, with a fresh array per row. Then write `paintCells(rows, cols, cells)` that starts from a grid of zeros and adds 1 to each listed `[r, c]` cell (cells may repeat). Ignore cells outside the grid, including negative coordinates. A zero or negative size gives an empty grid.
hints: `Array.from({ length: rows }, (_, r) => ...)` calls the mapper once per row, so each row can be a new array.
Type the callback as `(r: number, c: number) => T` and return `T[][]`; inference then gives `number[][]` for `() => 0`.
checklist: Painting one cell changes exactly one row.
Out-of-range and negative coordinates are ignored without throwing.
`makeGrid` infers `T` from the callback and contains no `any`.

extraPractice.title: Stable multi-key ranking
extraPractice.prompt: Write `rankRunners(runners)` for objects `{ name, time, bib }` where `time` is seconds or `null` for did-not-finish. Return names: finishers first by time ascending, equal times by bib ascending, then non-finishers by bib ascending. A time of `0` is a valid finish. Declare `type Comparator<T> = (a: T, b: T) => number` and a generic `thenBy(...comparators)` that returns the first non-zero result, and build the ranking from three small comparators. Do not mutate the input.
hints: Split the order into three comparators: finished before not finished (`Number(a.time === null) - Number(b.time === null)`), then time, then bib.
The time comparator must return 0 when either time is `null`; `Infinity - Infinity` is `NaN`, and a `NaN` result makes the order unreliable. Use `toSorted` to leave the input alone.
checklist: A time of `0` ranks as the fastest finisher, not as a non-finisher.
Non-finishers are ordered by bib, regardless of input order.
`thenBy` is typed `Comparator<T>[]` to `Comparator<T>`, and the input array is unchanged.

followUps.question: Why not use `Object.groupBy` or `Map.groupBy` in your answer?
followUps.answer: They arrived in ES2024. With an ES2023 target and lib they are neither typed nor guaranteed at runtime, so I would mention them and write the loop: get the bucket, create it if missing, push. Same O(n), and it works everywhere. If the environment is known to be current, `Map.groupBy(items, keyFn)` is the one-liner.

followUps.question: Your BFS uses `queue.shift()` and passes small tests but times out on a large grid. Why, and what do you change?
followUps.answer: `shift` removes the first element and moves all others down, O(n) per call, so the BFS becomes O(V²). Keep the array but read with a head index (`queue[head++]`) so dequeue is O(1). If memory matters for a long-running queue, compact periodically or use a fixed-size ring buffer.

followUps.question: When would you sort instead of using a heap for top-k?
followUps.answer: When the number of distinct items u is small or you need the full order anyway: sorting is O(u log u), simple and hard to get wrong. A size-k heap is O(u log k) and O(k) extra memory, which matters when u is huge, k is small, or items arrive as a stream. Quickselect gives average O(u) but is not stable and is fiddlier to write.

followUps.question: How do you reverse a string containing emoji?
followUps.answer: `s.split('').reverse()` reverses UTF-16 code units and breaks surrogate pairs. `[...s].reverse().join('')` reverses code points, which keeps single emoji intact. Combined sequences such as skin tones, flags or family emoji are several code points; reversing those correctly needs grapheme segmentation with `Intl.Segmenter`.

followUps.question: Your ids are 64-bit integers from an API. What can go wrong?
followUps.answer: `JSON.parse` turns them into `number`, and anything above 2^53 − 1 is rounded, so two ids can become equal. Keep them as strings in the JSON, or parse them to `bigint` explicitly. Remember that `bigint` does not mix with `number` arithmetic and `JSON.stringify` throws on a `bigint` unless you convert it.

takeaways: `fill` evaluates its argument once: build grids and bucket arrays with `Array.from({ length }, () => ...)`.
Callbacks receive (value, index, array); wrap functions such as `parseInt` that have optional parameters.
Use `for...of` for values; `for...in` yields string keys.
A head-index queue and a 40-line `MinHeap<T>` replace the missing deque and priority queue.
Comparators return numbers, chain explicit tie-breaks, and never subtract `null` or `Infinity`.
Know the number traps: float error, 2^53, remainder sign, `| 0` wrapping; reach for `bigint` or integer cents when exactness matters.

diagrams.title: fill(new Array()) versus Array.from per row
diagrams.alt: Comparison of two ways to build a three-row grid. On the left, new Array(3).fill(...) makes rows 0, 1 and 2 all point to one shared array, so a write through any row shows in all three. On the right, Array.from with a row factory gives each row index its own separate array.
diagrams.caption: `fill` evaluates its argument once and stores the same reference everywhere; a factory callback creates one array per row.

diagrams.title: What ['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt) really calls
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram with your code, Array.prototype.map and parseInt. Map calls parseInt three times, passing each string together with its index as the radix: parseInt('1', 0) returns 1, parseInt('2', 1) returns NaN and parseInt('3', 2) returns NaN, so the result is [1, NaN, NaN].
diagrams.caption: map passes (value, index, array); any callback with an optional second parameter gets the index whether you meant it or not.

messages.label: parseInt('1', 0, arr)
messages.note: The index 0 becomes the radix; 0 means "use the default", base 10.

messages.label: parseInt('2', 1, arr)
messages.note: Radix 1 is outside 2–36, so parseInt gives up.

messages.label: parseInt('3', 2, arr)
messages.note: '3' is not a binary digit, so nothing parses.

diagrams.title: Dequeuing 10,000 items: shift() versus a head index
diagrams.alt: Bar chart of element moves needed to dequeue 10,000 items one at a time. Calling shift each time models about 50 million element moves (n squared over 2), while reading with a head index needs about 0.01 million steps (n).
diagrams.caption: Big-O model from the spec, not a benchmark: shift moves every remaining element; a head index moves none. Engines may optimise small arrays, so do not count on it.

diagrams.title: push(1) into the min-heap [2, 5, 3, 9]
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram of a binary min-heap stored in an array, drawn as a tree: index 0 holds 2, index 1 holds 5, index 2 holds 3, index 3 holds 9. Pushing 1 appends it at index 4, a child of index 1. It swaps with 5 at index 1, then with 2 at index 0, and stops at the root. A note gives parent(i) = (i - 1) >> 1.
diagrams.caption: Append, then sift up while the new item beats its parent: at most one swap per level, O(log n).

steps.text: The array [2, 5, 3, 9] is a tree: children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, the parent is (i - 1) >> 1. Every parent is ≤ its children.
`push(1)` appends at index 4, the next free slot, so the tree stays complete.
The parent of 4 is 1, holding 5. `less(1, 5)` is true, so they swap: [2, 1, 3, 9, 5].
The parent of 1 is 0, holding 2. Swap again: [1, 2, 3, 9, 5]. Index 0 is the root, so stop.
`pop` runs the other way: take the root, move the last item to index 0 and sift it down to the smaller child until both children are larger.

diagrams.title: A comparator chain for runners
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram of a three-step comparator. compare(a, b) first checks finished status: if exactly one runner has no time, the finisher sorts first. Otherwise it compares times; a non-zero difference decides. On a tie it compares bib numbers, which are unique and settle every remaining case.
diagrams.caption: Each comparator either decides (non-zero) or passes to the next; the last key makes the order total.

steps.text: First key: `Number(a.time === null) - Number(b.time === null)`. If only one runner finished, it decides.
Second key: time. It returns 0 when either time is `null`, so it never produces `NaN`.
Last key: bib numbers are unique, so every pair is now ordered and the result does not depend on input order.

exercises.typeChecks:
type Equal<A, B> = (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false
type Expect<T extends true> = T
const h = new MinHeap<number>((a, b) => a < b)
h.push(3)
type _1 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof h.pop>, number | undefined>>
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof h.size, number>>
type _3 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof topKWords>, string[]>>
// @ts-expect-error a heap of numbers rejects a string
h.push('x')

type Equal<A, B> = (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false
type Expect<T extends true> = T
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Comparator<string>, (a: string, b: string) => number>>
const byLength = thenBy<string>((a, b) => a.length - b.length, (a, b) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0))
type _2 = Expect<Equal<typeof byLength, Comparator<string>>>
// @ts-expect-error a comparator returns a number, not a boolean
thenBy<string>((a, b) => a < b)

predict.explain: `map` passes the index as `parseInt`'s radix: radix 0 means default (1), radix 1 is invalid (NaN), and '3' is not a binary digit (NaN). Use `map(Number)`.
`Array(3)` has holes, which `map` and `filter` skip, so nothing survives. `Array.from` visits every index. `fill([])` stores one array in both slots, so the push shows twice.
`for...in` yields property keys, which are strings, so `'0' + 1` is `'01'`. `for...of` yields the values.

predict.code: console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, f: () => 1, n: NaN, xs: [undefined, () => 1, 2] }));
predict.explain: Object properties holding `undefined` or a function are omitted; inside an array they become `null` so indexes stay put. `NaN` serialises as `null`.
`%` keeps the sign of the dividend. `Math.trunc` rounds toward zero, `Math.floor` toward minus infinity. `| 0` converts to a signed 32-bit integer, so 3e9 wraps around.
The emoji is one code point but two UTF-16 units, so `length` is 4 and spreading gives 3. Months are 0-based: month 1 is February, and 31 February 2024 rolls over to 2 March (month 2).
Automatic semicolon insertion ends `return` at the line break, so the function returns `undefined` and `a + b` is unreachable. Keep the value on the same line as `return`.

lab.tip: Name the missing built-in before you write it: "JavaScript has no heap, so I'll write a 30-line `MinHeap` with a `less` function" or "no deque, so a head index". Then, before running, do a visible gotcha sweep aloud (`fill` with an object? `map(parseInt)`? a comparator that can return `NaN`?). It shows you know the language, not just the algorithm.
